sourceNote: Facts inspired by NASA DONKI, OSDR, and Mars weather archives. Simplified for junior astronauts.

solarFlares.name: M-Class Solar Flare
solarFlares.kidFact: The Sun sometimes sneezes energy toward Earth and space. An M-class flare is a medium sneeze!
solarFlares.effect: Radiation goes up. Hide in the shelter or boost shields.
solarFlares.donkiHint: DONKI tracks real solar storms for mission planners.

solarFlares.name: X-Class Solar Flare
solarFlares.kidFact: X-class flares are the biggest solar sneezes. They can scramble radios and raise radiation.
solarFlares.effect: Shielding drops fast. Pause outdoor work.
solarFlares.donkiHint: NASA watches X-flares closely before EVA walks.

solarFlares.name: Coronal Mass Ejection
solarFlares.kidFact: A CME is a giant bubble of Sun plasma racing through space—like a soap bubble of hot gas.
solarFlares.effect: Can hit days later. Plan extra power for life support.
solarFlares.donkiHint: DONKI lists CME arrival forecasts for crews.

martianDust.name: Local Dust Devil
martianDust.kidFact: Mars dust can spin into tiny tornadoes called dust devils. They look cool—but they coat solar panels!
martianDust.effect: Energy generation drops until panels are cleaned.
martianDust.scienceHint: Mars rovers measure dust opacity (how cloudy the sky gets).

martianDust.name: Regional Dust Storm
martianDust.kidFact: A dust storm can cover a whole region of Mars and block sunlight for days.
martianDust.effect: Solar power falls. Save energy for oxygen and water.
martianDust.scienceHint: Historic storms helped end some Mars missions that relied only on solar power.

martianDust.name: Planet-Encircling Dust
martianDust.kidFact: Sometimes dust wraps almost all of Mars. Days get dim like a dusty twilight.
martianDust.effect: Big energy shortage. Teamwork and careful budgets matter most.
martianDust.scienceHint: Global storms can last weeks and change the planet’s temperature.

radiationLimits.name: Daily Crew Limit
radiationLimits.kidFact: Radiation is invisible energy from space. Too much can hurt living things, so crews track it every day.
radiationLimits.safeRange: Keep shielding meter above 40% during calm space weather.
radiationLimits.osdrHint: OSDR studies how space radiation affects living systems.

radiationLimits.name: Flare Alert Threshold
radiationLimits.kidFact: When the Sun flares, radiation jumps. Going into a thick shelter is like putting on a space raincoat.
radiationLimits.safeRange: During flares, aim for shielding above 70%.
radiationLimits.osdrHint: NASA research helps design safer habitats and suits.

radiationLimits.name: Lunar Shadow Cold + Rays
radiationLimits.kidFact: On the Moon, two-week nights are freezing, and there is almost no air to block radiation.
radiationLimits.safeRange: Balance heat, power, and shields during long shadows.
radiationLimits.osdrHint: Moon missions practice living with long dark periods.

osdrFacts: Plants can grow in space greenhouses—but they need careful light, water, and air mixes.
Bones and muscles get weaker in microgravity, so astronauts exercise every day.
Water on a station is recycled from pee, sweat, and even cabin air moisture—science magic!
Sleep schedules matter: tired crews make riskier choices with power and oxygen.
Dust on the Moon sticks like chalk and can scratch seals if not cleaned.
Mars radio messages can take 3 to 22 minutes one way—no instant video calls!
Oxygen can be made from water with electricity—power and life support are best friends.
Science points come from experiments that help future explorers stay safer.

glossarySeed.definition: A Sol is one day on Mars. It is about 40 minutes longer than an Earth day.
A feeling of almost floating, like being weightless. On a station, things don't fall the way they do on Earth.
The systems that keep air, water, temperature, and pressure safe so people can live.
Extra-Vehicular Activity—fancy words for a spacewalk outside the base.
Invisible energy from the Sun and deep space. Too much is unsafe, so we use shielding.
A NASA space-weather tracker that watches solar flares and storms.
NASA's Open Science Data Repository—real research about living in space.
